title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: 55% of primary voters oppose data centers nearby — the debate over bills and water heats up.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight a new poll shows most Michigan primary voters want nothing to do with data centers in their own backyards, and the candidates are already fighting over who foots the bill.
That poll from today really lands, Graham. Fifty-five percent statewide say they oppose data centers nearby, and it jumps to sixty-three percent among likely Democratic primary voters.
Exactly. The survey highlights the split over higher electric bills and water use, and it comes as candidates stake out very different positions ahead of the August fourth primary.
So why is this opposition so strong right now? What's driving the numbers?

The concerns are pretty consistent across the state. Residents worry about who pays when these facilities pull hundreds of megawatts from the grid, and they worry about water draw in places that already face drought stress.
And farmland and small towns feel it too. Once a site goes in, the tax breaks and noise complaints follow.
Right. We've seen this play out in Saline Township, Coldwater, and now Genesee County. The poll just puts statewide numbers on what local meetings have been hearing for months.
How does this affect electric rates for regular households? I mean, if a data center takes a big chunk of power, does the rest of us pay more?
That's the core fight. Without new generation coming online fast enough, utilities often spread the cost across all customers. The poll shows voters are connecting those dots.
And water? Data centers use a lot for cooling, right?
They do, especially the larger ones. In rural townships that rely on wells or limited municipal supplies, that's a direct pressure point.
So the sixty-three percent among Democratic primary voters — is that because the candidates are making it a campaign issue?

It looks that way. Abdul El-Sayed held a rally Friday at the Saline site blasting tax breaks and grid strain. John James, the Republican Senate candidate, said yesterday he wants local officials to decide siting and taxes instead of state rules.
James wants to leave it to towns like Saline and Coldwater. That stance could play differently in data-center-heavy counties.
Exactly. Voters there are already litigating noise, power use, and tax incentives. The August fourth primary will test whether his hands-off approach helps or hurts.
And El-Sayed is using the same projects as proof that state-level deals are hurting residents thirty minutes away with higher rates.
Both sides are framing the same facilities differently. One side says local control protects communities; the other says it lets big projects slip through without enough oversight.
What happens next on the ground? We have several towns already hitting pause or delay.
Otsego city council voted Saturday to ban new data centers for a full year. That gives residents breathing room on noise and grid strain.
Genesee County also delayed its environmental clearance vote on Saturday. Extra weeks for public review on traffic, power, and industrial noise.
And Coldwater residents got their first public briefing Friday on proposed projects. They're asking the same questions about power draw, water, and tax breaks.
Meanwhile Dowagiac is shifting power from Bitcoin mining to a twenty-megawatt AI contract under a ten-year deal. That could bring over a billion dollars, but neighbors are still fighting the noise.
The facility at 415 East Prairie Ronde Street is already running around the clock, and residents describe a constant high-pitched whine.
That noise issue is shaping how Cass County handles future proposals. People want rules that protect sleep and property values.
Verrus is still pushing ahead on one Michigan site even while its Salem plans stall. Local officials are fielding questions about power and tax deals.
And Mason County is bidding to host the state's official data center. Rural western Michigan competing with bigger metro areas for jobs and tax revenue.
If it lands there, residents will face the same questions about land use and power demand that we've seen everywhere else.
So the poll numbers feel like they're reflecting real fatigue after months of these fights.
They do. And with the primary just two days away, candidates are racing to show they understand the stakes for everyday ratepayers and neighbors.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
More local meetings, more candidate stops at project sites, and probably more towns considering their own pauses or zoning changes.
The bigger picture is that data centers are no longer just an economic development story. They're now a pocketbook and quality-of-life issue for voters.
And the poll shows most primary voters have already made up their minds on that.
Let's move to the other stories from this week. John James told the Detroit News yesterday he'd leave data-center siting and tax decisions to local officials.
He specifically mentioned townships like Saline and Coldwater where fights over power, water, and tax breaks are already underway.
That position will get tested in those data-center-heavy counties on Tuesday.
Dowagiac's hyperscale site is reallocating twenty megawatts from Bitcoin to AI hosting. The ten-year deal could generate more than one point two billion dollars.
But the noise litigation from residents continues, so the community impact is still front and center.
Genesee County postponed its environmental approval vote on Saturday. Flint-area residents now have extra weeks to review traffic, power, and noise concerns.
Otsego enacted a one-year ban on new proposals Saturday. That pause lets the community shape rules before infrastructure gets strained.
Mason County is pitching itself for Michigan's official state data center. Construction jobs and tax revenue are the draw, but power and land-use questions remain.
Coldwater held a joint meeting Friday to brief residents on proposed data centers. Power, water, and tax breaks were the main topics.
Verrus is moving forward with its Michigan project while Salem plans stay uncertain. Local officials are already answering questions about demand and deals.
El-Sayed rallied Friday at the Saline site to criticize tax breaks and grid strain. He highlighted how projects thirty minutes away could raise rates for others.
And the Dowagiac noise complaints from Friday are now influencing how Cass County will handle future proposals.
Neighbors want protections for sleep and property values before more facilities arrive.
Now let's look ahead. On deck for tomorrow, Monday August third, the Delta County Planning Commission meets on its Data Center Subcommittee update and zoning ordinance discussion.
That's one listeners can actually attend if they're in the area or want to follow the local rules being shaped.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Voters Say No to Nearby Data Centers as Candidates Clash Over Costs
